title: I could not figure out why my live fills were always worse than my backtest. Then I realised I was filling on a candle that had not finished forming.
author: Electronic_Tea_2948
selftext:
This one took me months to catch and it was hiding in plain sight.

My backtest on a simple Nifty breakout was beautiful. Enter when price crosses above the previous candle’s high, clean equity curve, everything green. Live, it bled. Same rules, same instrument, totally different result. I assumed my execution was just sloppy.

So I sat and traced one trade by hand. In my backtest, my code was checking the 5 minute candle and entering at that candle’s close. Say the 9:30 candle closed at 24,210 after breaking the range, my backtest bought me in at exactly 24,210. But think about what that actually means in real life. To know the candle closed at 24,210, I have to wait for 9:35, when the candle is done. By then price is not sitting politely at 24,210 anymore. It has already moved to 24,224 or wherever. My backtest was buying at a price that only existed after the moment I could have acted.

That tiny gap was the whole problem. I was giving my backtest a price it could never actually get. Once I shifted my fills to the next candle’s open instead of the signal candle’s close, the gorgeous curve flattened out hard. The edge was never real. It was living inside a few points of impossible fills on every single trade.

Lesson I now live by. If a signal needs a candle to close, I cannot also trade at that close. The honest fill is the next open. Check your own engine for this, it quietly inflates everything.

How do you all handle signal-on-close versus fill timing? Next open, or something smarter?

comments.author: Maleficent-Success-6
comments.body:
Using the next candle's open is a much cleaner baseline when your signal requires the previous candle to close.

But I'd still distinguish the theoretical next open from the price your broker or exchange could actually execute.

For live comparison, I'd record three timestamps: when the completed candle became available, when the order was submitted, and when the fill actually occurred.

That makes it possible to separate signal timing errors from execution latency and slippage.

If you want to enter before the candle closes, that's a different strategy and needs intrabar data rather than information from the completed candle.

Have you checked whether your live and backtest signals now match exactly, independently of their execution prices?
